newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Gloom grows as no breakthrough in Yeltsin health.
newsitem.headline: Gloom grows as no breakthrough in Yeltsin health.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin was breathing more easily in hospital on Friday but there was no major breakthrough in fighting his pneumonia, a development that has deepened gloom over Russia's political health.

The Kremlin said the 65-year-old president's blood pressure and temperature were normal, despite a radio report quoting hospital sources as saying that inflammation of "medium gravity" had affected both of Yeltsin's lungs.

Russian newspapers offered a sober assessment of the political situation in Yeltsin's absence, saying the nuclear-armed state of 150 million people was leaderless and faced a period of stagnation in reforms.

"The president is breathing with more ease, there are less crepitations (crackling) in his lungs. The temperature remains normal, blood pressure is stable," a Kremlin statement said after doctors examined Yeltsin on Friday morning.
"But at the same time doctors think it is too early to speak about a breakthrough."

Yeltsin was taken to Moscow's elite Central Clinical Hospital on Wednesday evening. He had returned to the Kremlin just over two weeks earlier after an absence of nearly six months forced by cardiac problems culminating in a quintuple heart bypass operation on November 5.

Pneumonia, a serious infection or inflammation of the lungs, can affect one or both lungs. An infection of both lungs is considered more serious and difficult to treat, and the elderly are at greatest risk from the disease.
A Kremlin spokeswoman declined comment on the report by Moscow's Ekho Moskvy radio station that both of Yeltsin's lungs were inflamed.
Doctors have not said how long Yeltsin will have to spend in hospital or recovering before returning to the Kremlin.

Investors appeared unruffled by the concerns over Yeltsin's health. Enthusiastic buying sent Russian markets into record territory and Mosenergo, a bellwether stock, was up 14 percent for the day midway through the afternoon.
Alexander Lebed, one of Yeltsin's most outspoken political foes who finished third in last year's presidential vote, has said Yeltsin should step down. Some newspapers also expressed concern.
"President Sick, Premier On Holiday, Country All On Its Own", said a headline in the liberal daily Izvestia.
The liberal Nezavisimaya Gazeta declared: "The country is sicker than the president". It said setbacks in domestic and foreign policy could follow.

The Kremlin, anxious to portray Yeltsin as still engaged in state affairs, said on Thursday that he was in telephone contact with a number of Russian and foreign leaders and that he might speak to German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Friday.

Yeltsin is scheduled to host a meeting of leaders of the Commonwealth of Independent States in Moscow on January 17, but the Interfax news agency reported on Friday that the summit had been postponed until the end of the month. There was no immediate official confirmation of the report.
The Kremlin has played down Yeltsin's condition and says it has nothing to do with his heart bypass operation.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Yeltsin's constitutional deputy, was confident enough to begin a planned week's holiday near Moscow. He spoke on Thursday by telephone to Yeltsin, who is being treated with antibiotics.

Chernomyrdin, who would assume power for up to three months before elections if the president were to step down, took on wider responsibilities after Yeltsin was taken ill with heart trouble shortly before his re-election on July 3.

Pneumonia has struck a number of world leaders in recent months, including Czech President Vaclav Havel, religious leader Mother Teresa, and Austrian President Thomas Klestil, who spent seven weeks in the hospital with a severe case.
Greek Prime Minister Andreas Papandreou resigned in January last year after spending eight weeks in hospital with the illness. He died in June of a heart attack.
